label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
    There exist an absolute constant $c>0$ and an integer $d_0\ge1$ such that,
    for every integer $d\ge d_0$, we have 
    $$
    \Delta_d^L
    \ge
    c\,d^2\log\log d\,2^{-d}.
    $$
head: environment

label: ex:two-component-gluing
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:two-component-gluing}
    Take $\mathcal N=\{1,3\}.$
    Then
    $$
    \mathcal A
    =
    \mathbb Z[X]/\bigl((X-1)\Phi_3(X)\bigr)
    \hookrightarrow
    \mathcal O
    =
    \mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z[\zeta_3].
    $$
    Writing $\beta=m+n\zeta_3$, a pair
    $(a,\beta)\in\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z[\zeta_3]$ lies in the image of
    $\mathcal A$ precisely when
    $$
    a\equiv m+n\pmod 3.
    $$
    In particular, if $a=0$, so that the element is supported only on the cyclotomic component corresponding to $n=3$, then
    $
    m+n\equiv0\pmod3.
    $
    Equivalently, the possible values of $\beta$ form the sublattice
    $
    (1-\zeta_3)\mathbb Z[\zeta_3]
    \subset \mathbb Z[\zeta_3],
    $
    which has index $3$, since
    $
    \mathbb Z[\zeta_3]\big/
    (1-\zeta_3)\mathbb Z[\zeta_3]
    \simeq \mathbb F_3.
    $
    The point of the example is that forcing one cyclotomic component to
    vanish imposes a nontrivial restriction on the remaining component.
    Indeed, it forces it into a proper sublattice.  This gluing condition is illustrated in \cref{fig:two-component-gluing}.
head: environment
name: Gluing of two components

label: lem:orbit
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:orbit}
    Let $0\ne v\in\mathcal A\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ with support
    $S\subset\mathcal N$. Then
    $$
    \#\operatorname{Orb}(v)
    =
    M_S.
    $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $n\in S$, the $n$-th component is fixed by $\tau^j$ if and only if
    $\zeta_n^j=1$, equivalently $n\mid j$.  Hence $v$ is fixed by
    $\tau^j$ precisely when $j$ is divisible by every $n\in S$.  The
    least positive such $j$ is
    $
    \operatorname{lcm}\{n:n\in S\}.
    $
head: environment

label: lem:support-index
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:support-index}
    We have
    $$
    [\mathcal O:\mathcal A]=I_{\mathrm{all}},
    $$
    and, for every $S\subset\mathcal N$,
    $$
    [\mathcal O_S:\mathcal A\cap K_S]
    =
    I_{\mathrm{internal}}(S)I_{\mathrm{cross}}(S).
    $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first identity follows by computing the determinant of the evaluation map
    $
    \mathbb Z[X]/(F)
    \to
    \bigoplus_{n\in\mathcal N}\mathbb Z[\zeta_n].
    $
    With respect to the monomial basis on the left and the power basis of each
    cyclotomic ring on the right, its determinant is, up to sign,
    $
    \prod_{\{m,n\}\subset\mathcal N}
    \operatorname{Res}(\Phi_m,\Phi_n).
    $
    Taking absolute values therefore gives
    $
    [\mathcal O:\mathcal A]=I_{\mathrm{all}}.
    $
    Now fix $S\subset\mathcal N$ and set
    $$
    F_{S^c}=\prod_{n\notin S}\Phi_n,
    \qquad
    \mathcal A_S=\mathbb Z[X]\Big/\Bigl(\prod_{m\in S}\Phi_m\Bigr),
    $$
    viewing $\mathcal A_S$ as an order in $K_S$ via evaluation.
    An element of $\mathcal A$ lies in $K_S$ precisely when its polynomial
    representative vanishes at every $\zeta_n$ with $n\notin S$, or
    equivalently is divisible by $F_{S^c}$.  Hence
    $
    \mathcal A\cap K_S=F_{S^c}\mathcal A_S.
    $
    By the first identity, we have 
    $
    [\mathcal O_S:\mathcal A_S]=I_{\mathrm{internal}}(S).
    $
    For a number field $K$, write $N_{K/\mathbb Q}$ for its field norm.
    Multiplication by $F_{S^c}$ on the $m$-th component has absolute 
    determinant
    $$
    \left|N_{K_m/\mathbb Q}\bigl(F_{S^c}(\zeta_m)\bigr)\right|
    =
    \prod_{n\notin S}
    \left|N_{K_m/\mathbb Q}\bigl(\Phi_n(\zeta_m)\bigr)\right|
    =
    \prod_{n\notin S}
    \left|\operatorname{Res}(\Phi_m,\Phi_n)\right|,
    $$
    so taking the product over $m\in S$ gives
    $
    [\mathcal A_S:F_{S^c}\mathcal A_S]
    =I_{\mathrm{cross}}(S).
    $
    Multiplicativity of index now gives the result.

label: lem:supportwise-mean
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Logarithm of the mean for a prescribed support

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\lambda T_y g$ preserves cyclotomic support, we have 
    $$
    \begin{aligned}
        \mathbb E_g
        \left|\left\{
            x\in\Lambda_g^*\cap B_s:
            \operatorname{supp}(x)=S
        \right\}\right| 
        =
        \mathbb E_g
        \sum_{v\in L_S^\circ}
        \mathbf1_{B_s}\bigl(\lambda T_ygv\bigr).
    \end{aligned}
    $$
    Applying \cref{lem:mean} with
    $
    f(u)
    =
    \mathbf1_{B_s}\bigl(\lambda T_yu\bigr)
    $
    gives
    $$
    \mathbb E_g
    \left|\left\{
        x\in\Lambda_g^*\cap B_s:
        \operatorname{supp}(x)=S
    \right\}\right|
    =
    \frac{
        \operatorname{vol}\bigl((\lambda T_y|_{V_S})^{-1}B_s\bigr)
    }{
        \operatorname{covol}(L_S)
    }.
    $$
    Now
    $$
    \det(T_y|_{V_S})
    =
    \exp\left(
        \sum_{n\in S}
        \bigl(rc_n+a\mathbf1_{\{n=1\}}\bigr)\widetilde y_n
    \right),
    $$
    while
    $
    \operatorname{covol}(L_S)=e^{rI_{\mathrm{inc}}(S)}.
    $
    Therefore
    $$
    \begin{aligned}
        \mathbb E_g
        \left|\left\{
            x\in\Lambda_g^*\cap B_s:
            \operatorname{supp}(x)=S
        \right\}\right|
        =
        v_s\lambda^{-s}
        \exp\left(
            -rI_{\mathrm{inc}}(S)
            -
            \sum_{n\in S}
            \bigl(rc_n+a\mathbf1_{\{n=1\}}\bigr)\widetilde y_n
        \right).
    \end{aligned}
    $$
    Taking logarithms and using
    $$
    -s\log\lambda
    =
    -\frac{s}{d}\log v_d
    +\frac{s}{d}rI
    $$
    gives \eqref{eq:finite-support}.
head: environment

label: lem:support-exponent-comparison
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:support-exponent-comparison}
    Suppose that $I/C \ll\log C$ and $|y_1|\ll\log C.$ 
    Then there exists an absolute constant $K>0$ such that, for every nonempty
    $S\subseteq\mathcal N$,

    $$
    \mathcal L(S)
    \le
    r\mathscr A(S)+KC\log d.
    $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Starting from \eqref{eq:finite-support}, we compare each term with the
    corresponding term in $r\mathscr A(S)$. First, Stirling's formula gives, uniformly for $1\le s\le d$,
    $$
    \log v_s-\frac{s}{d}\log v_d
    \le
    \frac{s}{2}\log\frac ds+O(\log d).
    $$
    Since
    $$
    s=rc_S+a\varepsilon_S,
    \qquad
    d=Cr+a,
    \qquad
    0\le a<C,
    $$
    we obtain
    $$
    \frac{s}{2}\log\frac ds
    =
    r\frac{c_S}{2}\log\frac C{c_S}
    +O(C\log d).
    $$
    Next,
    $$
    \frac{s}{d}
    =
    \frac{rc_S+a\varepsilon_S}{Cr+a}
    =
    \frac{c_S}{C}
    +O\!\left(\frac1r\right).
    $$
    Therefore, using the assumed bound $I/C\ll\log C$, we get 
    $$
    \frac{s}{d}rI
    =
    r\frac{c_S}{C}I
    +O(I)
    =
    r\frac{c_S}{C}I
    +O(C\log d).
    $$
    The term involving $\operatorname{covol}(L_S)$ requires no approximation. For the componentwise scaling term, recall that
    $
    \widetilde y_n=y_n-\eta$ and 
    $
    \eta=\frac{ay_1}{d}.
    $
    Using
    $
    s
    =
    \sum_{n\in S}
    \bigl(rc_n+a\mathbf1_{\{n=1\}}\bigr)
    =
    rc_S+a\varepsilon_S,
    $
    we obtain
    \begin{align*}
        \sum_{n\in S}
        \bigl(rc_n+a\mathbf1_{{n=1}}\bigr)\widetilde y_n
        -
        r\sum_{n\in S}c_ny_n
        =
        a\varepsilon_Sy_1-\eta s
        =
        ay_1
        \left(
            \varepsilon_S-\frac{s}{d}
        \right).
    \end{align*}
    Since $0\le s/d\le1$ and $\varepsilon_S\in\{0,1\}$, we have 
    $
    \left|
    \varepsilon_S-\frac{s}{d}
    \right|
    \le1.
    $
    Thus
    $$
    \left|
    \sum_{n\in S}
    \bigl(rc_n+a\mathbf1_{\{n=1\}}\bigr)\widetilde y_n
    -
    r\sum_{n\in S}c_ny_n
    \right|
    \le
    a|y_1|.
    $$
    The assumption $|y_1|\ll\log C$ and $a<C$ implies that 
    $$
    \sum_{n\in S}
    \bigl(rc_n+a\mathbf1_{\{n=1\}}\bigr)\widetilde y_n
    =
    r\sum_{n\in S}c_ny_n
    +O(C\log d),
    $$
    uniformly in $S$. Substituting these estimates into \eqref{eq:finite-support} gives
    $$
    \mathcal L(S)
    \le
    r
    \left[
        \frac{c_S}{2}\log\frac C{c_S}
        +\frac{c_S}{C}I
        -I_{\mathrm{inc}}(S)
        -\sum_{n\in S}c_ny_n
    \right]
    +KC\log d
    $$
    for some absolute constant $K>0$, uniformly in $S$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
For each sufficiently large integer $d$, let
    $\mathcal N \subset\mathbb N$ be a finite index set with
    $1\in\mathcal N$ and $2\notin\mathcal N$, and put
    $$
    C=\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}c_n,
    \qquad
    M=\operatorname{lcm}\{n:n\in\mathcal N\}.
    $$
    Write
    $$
    r=\left\lfloor\frac{d}{C}\right\rfloor,
    \qquad
    d=C r+a,
    \qquad
    0\le a<C.
    $$
    For $n\in\mathcal N$, let $y_{n}$ be real numbers. We call the family $\left(\mathcal N,(y_{n})_{n\in\mathcal N}\right)$ admissible if there exists an absolute constant $\delta>0$ such that
    $$
    \sum_{n\in\mathcal N}c_n y_{n}=0,
    \qquad
    \mathscr A(S)\le-\delta
    $$
    for every nonempty proper $S\subsetneq\mathcal N$, together with 
    $$
    \frac{I}{C}\ll\log C,
    \qquad
    |y_{1}|\ll\log C,
    \qquad 
    r\gg C^3\log d,
    \qquad
    C\ge\log d,
    \qquad
    \log M\ll\log d.
    $$
    All implied constants and $\delta$ are required to be uniform in $d$.
head: environment
name: Admissible family of gluing data

label: lem:fixed-support
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:fixed-support}
    There exists $d_0$ such that, for every $d\ge d_0$ and every nonempty proper support $\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq\mathcal N, $ we have
    $$
    \mathcal L(S)
    \le
    -\frac34\delta r. 
    $$
    Equivalently,
    $$
    \mathbb E_g
    \left|\left\{
        x\in\Lambda_g^*\cap B_s:
        \operatorname{supp}(x)=S
    \right\}\right|
    \le
    e^{-3\delta r/4}.
    $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $S$ is a nonempty proper support, \cref{lem:support-exponent-comparison} and the uniform gluing condition give
    $$
    \mathcal L(S)
    \le
    -\delta r+KC\log d.
    $$
    Using the admissibility
    $
    r\gg C^3\log d
    $
    gives 
    $
    \frac{C\log d}{r}
    \ll
    \frac1{C^2}
    \to 0.
    $
    Thus, for all sufficiently large $d$, we have 
    $$
    KC\log d
    \le
    \frac{\delta}{4}r.
    $$
    This proves the claimed bound.
head: environment

label: cor:proper-supports
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a support $S$ of real dimension $s$, replacing the unit ball by
    $B_\rho$ changes $\mathcal L(S)$ by
    $
    s\log\rho.
    $
    Since $s\le d$, \eqref{eq:rho-range} gives
    $
    |s\log\rho|
    \ll
    1+d\sqrt{\frac{\log d}{r}}.
    $
    Since
    $
    d=Cr+a
    \le C(r+1),
    $
    we obtain
    $
    |s\log\rho|
    \ll
    1+C\sqrt{r\log d}.
    $
    The admissibility condition 
    $
    r\gg C^3\log d
    $
    gives 
    $$
    \frac{
        C\sqrt{r\log d}
    }{r}
    =
    C\sqrt{\frac{\log d}{r}}
    \ll
    \frac1{\sqrt C}
    \to 0.
    $$
    Thus the change in $\mathcal L(S)$ is $o(r)$, uniformly in $S$.
    By \cref{lem:fixed-support}, for all sufficiently large $d$, the Haar
    expected number of vectors in $B_\rho$ with any fixed nonempty proper
    support is therefore, say, at most
    $
    e^{-\delta r/2}.
    $

    It remains only to count the possible supports.  Since
    $
    c_n=\varphi(n)\ge1
    $
    for every $n\in\mathcal N$, we have 
    $
    |\mathcal N|
    \le
    \sum_{n\in\mathcal N}c_n
    =
    C.
    $
    Hence the number of supports is at most
    $
    2^{|\mathcal N|}
    \le
    2^C.
    $
    Moreover,
    $$
    \frac Cr
    \ll
    \frac{1}{C^2\log d}
    \to 0
    $$
    gives 
    $
    C\log2=o(r).
    $
    Summing the estimates over all supports gives
    $
    2^C e^{-\delta r/2}
    \le
    e^{-cr}
    $
    for some absolute $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $d$.

body_md:

label: lem:entropy-tensorization
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let
    $
    \mu_j(x_j)=\frac{c_j(x_j)}{C_j}
    $
    be the probability measure on $X_j$ and let
    $
    \mu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^J\mu_j
    $
    be the product measure on $X$. By the product structure we have 
    $$
    \mu(x)=\prod_{j=1}^J\frac{c_j(x_j)}{C_j} = \frac{c(x)}{C},
    \qquad
    \mu(S)=\frac{c(S)}{C}.
    $$
    The entropy tensorization inequality
    \cite[Eq.~(1.2)]{CaputoMenzTetali2015}, applied to $f=1_S$, is
    $$
    \operatorname{Ent}_\mu(1_S)
    \le
    \sum_{j=1}^J
    \mu\!\left[\operatorname{Ent}_{\mu_j}(1_S)\right].
    $$
    Since
    $
    \operatorname{Ent}_\mu(1_S)
    =
    \mu(S)\log(1/\mu(S)),
    $
    the left-hand side becomes
    $$
    \frac C2\,\operatorname{Ent}_\mu(1_S)
    =
    \frac{c(S)}{2}\log\frac{C}{c(S)}.
    $$
    For $u\in X_{-j}$ we have 
    $$
    \operatorname{Ent}_{\mu_j}(1_{S_{j,u}})
    =
    \frac{c_j(S_{j,u})}{C_j}
    \log\frac{C_j}{c_j(S_{j,u})},
    \qquad
    \mu_{-j}(u)
    =
    \frac{c_{-j}(u)}{C/C_j}.
    $$
    Hence
    $$
    \begin{aligned}
        \mu\!\left[\operatorname{Ent}_{\mu_j}(1_S)\right]
        =
        \sum_{u\in X_{-j}}
        \mu_{-j}(u)\,
        \operatorname{Ent}_{\mu_j}(1_{S_{j,u}}) 
        =
        \frac1C
        \sum_{u\in X_{-j}}
        c_{-j}(u)c_j(S_{j,u})
        \log\frac{C_j}{c_j(S_{j,u})}.
    \end{aligned}
    $$
    Multiplying the tensorization inequality by $C/2$ gives the claim.
head: environment

label: lem:product-support
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:product-support}
    For $1\le j\le J$, let $X_j$ be finite weighted graphs with positive
    integer vertex weights $c_j$, edge weight functions $w_j$, total
    weights $C_j$, and potentials $v_j$ satisfying
    $
    \sum_{x_j\in X_j}c_j(x_j)v_j(x_j)=0.
    $
    Suppose that, for some $\delta>0$,
    $
    \mathcal E_{X_j}(U)\le-\delta
    $
    for every $j$ and every nonempty proper $U\subsetneq X_j$.

    Equip
    $
    X=\prod_{j=1}^JX_j
    $
    with the vertex weights
    $
    c(x)=\prod_{j=1}^Jc_j(x_j)
    $
    and potential
    $
    v(x)=\sum_{j=1}^Jv_j(x_j).
    $
    Give $X$ the product weighted graph in which two vertices are adjacent if they
    differ in exactly one coordinate, say the $j$-th, and such an edge has
    weight
    $$
    \left(\prod_{i\ne j}c_i(x_i)\right)
    w_j(x_j,x_j').
    $$
    Then $v$ has weighted mean zero and
    $
    \mathcal E_X(S)\le-\delta
    $
    for every nonempty proper $S\subsetneq X$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have 
    $$
    \begin{aligned}
        \sum_{x\in X}c(x)v(x)
&=
\sum_{j=1}^J
\left(\prod_{i\ne j}C_i\right)
\sum_{x_j\in X_j}c_j(x_j)v_j(x_j)
=0,
    \end{aligned}
    $$
    so the product potential has weighted mean zero.

    Now fix $S\subseteq X$. \cref{lem:entropy-tensorization} gives 
    $$
    \frac{c(S)}2\log\frac{C}{c(S)}
    \le
    \sum_{j=1}^J
    \sum_{u\in X_{-j}}
    c_{-j}(u)
    \frac{c_j(S_{j,u})}{2}
    \log\frac{C_j}{c_j(S_{j,u})}.
    $$
    By the definition of the product graph, the boundary term decomposes as
    $$
    W_X(S,S^c)
    =
    \sum_{j=1}^J
    \sum_{u\in X_{-j}}
    c_{-j}(u)
    W_j(S_{j,u},S_{j,u}^c).
    $$
    Likewise we have 
    $$
    \sum_{x\in S}c(x)v(x)
    =
    \sum_{j=1}^J
    \sum_{u\in X_{-j}}
    c_{-j}(u)
    \sum_{x_j\in S_{j,u}}
    c_j(x_j)v_j(x_j).
    $$
    Combining these three relations gives
    $$
    \mathcal E_X(S)
    \le
    \sum_{j=1}^J
    \sum_{u\in X_{-j}}
    c_{-j}(u)\,
    \mathcal E_{X_j}(S_{j,u}).
    $$
    If $S_{j,u}=\varnothing$, then
    $\mathcal E_{X_j}(S_{j,u})=0$.  The same is true when
    $S_{j,u}=X_j$, by the zero-mean condition on $v_j$.
    Every nonempty proper fiber, on the other hand, satisfies
    $
    \mathcal E_{X_j}(S_{j,u})\le-\delta.
    $
    Suppose now that $S$ is nonempty and proper.  Choose
    $x\in S$ and $x'\notin S$, and replace the coordinates of $x$ by
    those of $x'$ one at a time.  At some step one passes from $S$ to
    $S^c$.  The corresponding fiber $S_{j,u}$ is therefore nonempty and
    proper.  Since the vertex weights are positive integers,
    $
    c_{-j}(u)\ge1.
    $
    Hence at least one term in the preceding sum is at most $-\delta$, while
    all the others are nonpositive.  Therefore
    $
    \mathcal E_X(S)\le-\delta.
    $

label: lem:divisor-cube-entropy
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set
    $
    \mu(B):=\frac{\rho(B)}{P}.
    $
    Then
    $$
    \mu(B)
    =
    \prod_{p\in B}\frac1p
    \prod_{p\in\mathcal P\setminus B}\frac{p-1}{p},
    $$
    so $\mu$ is obtained by including each $p\in\mathcal P$
    independently with probability $1/p$.
    Let $f=\mathbf1_{\mathcal U}$.  Entropy tensorization gives
    $$
    \operatorname{Ent}_\mu(f)
    \le
    \sum_{p\in\mathcal P}
    \mathbb E_{\mu_{-p}}\!\left[\operatorname{Ent}_{\mu_p}(f)\right].
    $$
    For fixed $p$, a choice of the remaining primes is a set
    $B\subseteq\mathcal P\setminus\{p\}$.  Varying whether $p$ is
    included gives the cube edge
    $
    B\longleftrightarrow B\cup\{p\}.
    $
    If this edge does not cross the boundary of $\mathcal U$, then $f$
    has the same value at its two endpoints and hence contributes zero
    entropy.  If it does cross the boundary, then $f$ takes the values
    $0$ and $1$. The endpoint at which
    $f=1$ has probability either $1/p$ or $(p-1)/p$
    and in either case its entropy is at most
    $
    (\log p)/p.
    $ 

    The probability of the choice $B$ outside the $p$-coordinate is
    $$
    \mu_{-p}(B)
    =
    \prod_{p'\in B}\frac1{p'}
    \prod_{p'\in\mathcal P\setminus(B\cup\{p\})}\frac{p'-1}{p'}.
    $$
    Hence
    $$
    \operatorname{Ent}_\mu(f)
    \le
    \sum_{\substack{p\in\mathcal P,\,
            B\subseteq\mathcal P\setminus\{p\}\\
            B\leftrightarrow B\cup\{p\}
    \text{ crosses }\partial\mathcal U}}
    \mu_{-p}(B)\frac{\log p}{p}.
    $$
    But
    $$
    P\,\mu_{-p}(B)\frac{\log p}{p}
    =
    \rho(B\cup\{p\})\log p,
    $$
    which is exactly the weight of the edge
    $B\leftrightarrow B\cup\{p\}$. Summing over all such crossing edges gives
    $
    P\,\operatorname{Ent}_\mu(f)
    \le
    E_{\mathcal P}(\mathcal U).
    $
    Combining this with 
    $   P\operatorname{Ent}_\mu(\mathbf1_{\mathcal U})
    =
    u(\mathcal U)\log\frac{P}{u(\mathcal U)}
    $
    proves the claim.
head: environment

label: lem:cube-linear-bound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cube-linear-bound}
    If $\varnothing\notin\mathcal U\subseteq2^{\mathcal P}$, then
    $$
    E_{\mathcal P}(\mathcal U)
    \ge
    \frac{\ell}{P}\,u(\mathcal U),
    \qquad
    \ell:=\min_{p\in\mathcal P}\log p.
    $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an ordering of the primes in $\mathcal P$.  For each
    $B\in\mathcal U$, consider the path from $B$ to $\varnothing$
    obtained by removing the primes of $B$ one at a time in this order. Give this path weight $\rho(B)$.  Since
    $\varnothing\notin\mathcal U$, every such path crosses the boundary
    of $\mathcal U$.

    Consider a cube edge obtained by removing one prime,
    $$
    D\longleftrightarrow D\setminus\{p\},
    \qquad D\subseteq\mathcal P,\quad p\in D.
    $$  Only paths starting at sets $B\supseteq D$ can use this edge. Since every $B\supseteq D$ is uniquely of the form
    $B=D\cup C$, with $C\subseteq\mathcal P\setminus D$, we have
    $$
    \sum_{B\supseteq D}\rho(B)
    =
    \rho(D)
    \prod_{p'\in\mathcal P\setminus D}\frac {p'}{p'-1}
    \le
    P\rho(D).
    $$ 
    On the other hand, since the edge has weight
    $
    \rho(D)\log p\ge \ell\rho(D),
    $
    we obtain
    $$
    P\rho(D)
    \le
    \frac{P}{\ell}
    \bigl(\text{weight of the edge}\bigr).
    $$  Since every path crosses the boundary of
    $\mathcal U$, summing over the boundary edges gives
    $$
    u(\mathcal U)
    \le
    \frac{P}{\ell}E_{\mathcal P}(\mathcal U),
    $$
    as claimed.

label: eq:normalized-one-block
title: Proof
body_md:
We normalize by $\varphi(qN)$ and write
    $$
    s(U):=\frac{c_U}{\varphi(qN)}
    =\sum_{x\in U}\lambda(x),
    \qquad
    Z:=\frac{C_{\mathrm{loc}}}{\varphi(qN)},
    \qquad
    E(U):=\frac{W(U,U^c)}{\varphi(qN)}.
    $$
    Thus it is enough to prove
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{s(U)}2\log\frac{Z}{s(U)}
        -\frac12E(U)
        -\sum_{x\in U}\lambda(x)v_x
        \le
        -\delta_0\min\{s(U),Z-s(U)\}.
        \label{eq:normalized-one-block}
    \end{equation}
    The cases $U=\varnothing$ and
    $U=\mathcal D(q;N)$ are immediate. Suppose first that $F\notin U$, so $U$ consists only of divisors
    of $N$.  For $n\mid N$, let
    $
    B(n):=\{p\in\mathcal P:p\nmid n\}
    $
    be the set of primes omitted from $n$, and put
    $
    \mathcal U:=\{B(n):n\in U\}$ and  $u:=u(\mathcal U).$ 
    Since $\lambda(n)=a\rho(B(n))$, we have $
    s(U)=au.
    $
    Put 
    $
    \varepsilon:=\mathbf1_{\{N\in U\}}.
    $
    The boundary of $U$ consists of edges of the divisor cube with one endpoint in $U$ and one outside
    $U$, and possibly the additional edge $N$--$F$. The normalized
    weights of the cube edges are $a$ times the weights used in
    $E_{\mathcal P}$, while the normalized weight of $N$--$F$ is
    $a\log q$.  Hence
    $$
    E(U)
    =
    aE_{\mathcal P}(\mathcal U)
    +a\varepsilon\log q.
    $$ 
    Moreover, by \eqref{eq:local-potential}, we have 
    $$
    \sum_{x\in U}\lambda(x)v_x
    =
    \frac{s(U)\Theta}{2}
    +\delta_0s(U)
    -\frac{a\varepsilon\log q}{2}.
    $$
    We also note that 
    $$
    \log\frac{Z}{s(U)}
    =
    \Theta+\log\frac{P}{u}.
    $$
    Substituting these identities into the left-hand side of
    \eqref{eq:normalized-one-block}, the terms involving $\Theta$ and
    $\varepsilon\log q$ cancel, and we obtain
    \begin{align} \label{eq:non-pos}
        \frac a2
        \left(
            u\log\frac Pu-E_{\mathcal P}(\mathcal U)
        \right)
        -\delta_0s(U).
    \end{align}
    By Lemma~\ref{lem:divisor-cube-entropy}, the term in parentheses is nonpositive.
    Hence  \eqref{eq:non-pos} is at most
    $
    -\delta_0s(U).
    $
    Since $s(U)\le aP<1$ while $Z-s(U)\ge1$, we have
    $$
    \min\{s(U),Z-s(U)\}=s(U),
    $$
    which proves \eqref{eq:normalized-one-block} when $F\notin U$.

    Now suppose that $F\in U$ and let $
    V:=\mathcal D(q;N)\setminus U.
    $
    Then $V\neq\varnothing$ and $F\notin V$. Put
    $$
    s:=s(V),
    \qquad
    \mathcal V:=\{B(n):n\in V\},
    \qquad
    \varepsilon:=\mathbf1_{\{N\in V\}},
    $$
    where $B(n)$ is as above.  Since the same edges cross the
    boundaries of $U$ and $V$, we have 
    $
    E(U)=E(V).
    $ Moreover,
    \eqref{eq:local-potential-zero} gives
    $$
    \sum_{x\in U}\lambda(x)v_x
    =
    -\sum_{x\in V}\lambda(x)v_x.
    $$
    Using
    $$
    (Z-s)\log\frac{Z}{Z-s}\le s,
    $$
    and applying the formulas from the first case to $V$, we obtain 
    \begin{equation}
        \begin{aligned}
&\frac{Z-s}{2}\log\frac{Z}{Z-s}
-\frac12E(V)
+\sum_{x\in V}\lambda(x)v_x \\
&\qquad\le
\frac s2
-\frac a2E_{\mathcal P}(\mathcal V)
+\frac{s\Theta}{2}
+\delta_0s
-a\varepsilon\log q.
        \end{aligned}
        \label{eq:complement-local-bound}
    \end{equation}
    If $\varepsilon=0$, then $N\notin V$, and hence
    $\varnothing\notin\mathcal V$. 
    \cref{lem:cube-linear-bound} then gives 
    $$
    E_{\mathcal P}(\mathcal V)
    \ge
    \frac{\ell}{P}u(\mathcal V)
    =
    \frac{\ell}{aP}s.
    $$
    Therefore the right-hand side of
    \eqref{eq:complement-local-bound} is at most
    $$
    \frac s2
    \left(
        1+\Theta+2\delta_0-\frac{\ell}{P}
    \right)
    \le
    -\delta_0s,
    $$
    where we used \eqref{eq:good-local-block} and
    $\Theta\le\log q$.

    Finally, suppose that $\varepsilon=1$.  Then the edge $N$--$F$
    crosses the boundary of $V$.  Since $E_{\mathcal P}(\mathcal V)\ge0$, we may discard the
    nonpositive second term in \eqref{eq:complement-local-bound}. Using $s\le aP$, we get
    $$
    \eqref{eq:complement-local-bound}
    \le
    \frac{aP}{2}(1+\Theta+2\delta_0)-a\log q.
    $$
    Since $P\le5/4$ and $\Theta\le\log q$, this is at most
    $
    -\delta_0aP
    \le
    -\delta_0s
    $
    for all sufficiently large $q$. This proves \eqref{eq:normalized-one-block}, and hence
    \eqref{eq:one-block-support}.

label: lem:angular
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:angular}
    Let $\omega$ be uniformly distributed on $S^{d-1}$.  Then
    $$
    \mathbb E
    \bigl\|
    \Pi(\omega\otimes\omega)
    \bigr\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
    =
    \frac{2q+d}{d(d+2)}.
    $$
    Moreover, there are absolute constants $c,K>0$ such that, whenever
    $$
    0\le\lambda
    \le
    c\sqrt{\frac{2q+d}{d}},
    $$
    we have
    $$
    \mathbb E
    \exp\left(
        \lambda
        \frac{d(d+2)}{2q+d}
        \bigl\|
        \Pi(\omega\otimes\omega)
        \bigr\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
    \right)
    \le
    K e^\lambda.
    $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For any real symmetric matrix $B$, let
    $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$ be its eigenvalues. By rotational
    invariance, we may assume
    $B=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)$. Using
    $$
    \mathbb E\omega_i^4=\frac{3}{d(d+2)},
    \qquad
    \mathbb E(\omega_i^2\omega_j^2)=\frac{1}{d(d+2)}
    \quad (i\ne j),
    $$
    we obtain
    $$
    \begin{aligned}
        \mathbb E\langle B\omega,\omega\rangle^2
        =
        \frac{
            3\sum_i\lambda_i^2
            +2\sum_{i<j}\lambda_i\lambda_j
        }{d(d+2)}
        =
        \frac{
            2\operatorname{Tr}(B^2)
            +\operatorname{Tr}(B)^2
        }{d(d+2)}.
    \end{aligned}
    $$
    Summing the preceding identity gives
    $$
    \mathbb E
    \bigl\|
    \Pi(\omega\otimes\omega)
    \bigr\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
    = 
    \frac{
        2q+
        \sum_{j=1}^q\operatorname{Tr}(B_j)^2
    }{d(d+2)}.
    $$
    Since $\operatorname{Tr}(B_j)=\langle B_j,\operatorname{Id}_d\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}$
    and $\operatorname{Id}_d\in\mathcal Q$, Parseval gives
    $
    \sum_{j=1}^q \operatorname{Tr}(B_j)^2
    =
    \|\operatorname{Id}_d\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
    =
    d,
    $
    which proves the first assertion.

    Set
    $$
    F(\omega)
    =
    \sqrt{
        \frac{d(d+2)}{2q+d}
    }\,
    \bigl\|
    \Pi(\omega\otimes\omega)
    \bigr\|_{\mathrm{HS}}.
    $$
    Then $\mathbb EF^2=1.$ Moreover, for $u,v\in S^{d-1}$ we have  $ \|u\otimes u-v\otimes v\|_{\mathrm{HS}} \le 2\|u-v\|.$ Since orthogonal projection is contractive in Hilbert--Schmidt norm, it follows
    that $F(\omega)$ is $L$-Lipschitz on $S^{d-1}$, with Lipschitz constant 
    $$
    L
    \le
    2\sqrt{\frac{d(d+2)}{2q+d}}.
    $$

    By the concentration inequality for Lipschitz functions on the sphere
    (see, for example, \cite[Theorem~5.1.3]{VershyninHDP}), there is an absolute constant
    $c_0>0$ such that
    $$
    \Pr\{|F-\mathbb EF|>s\}
    \le
    2\exp\left(-c_0\frac{d}{L^2}s^2\right),
    \qquad s\ge0.
    $$
    Since $\mathbb EF^2=1$, Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\mathbb EF\le1.$ Since 
    $
    \frac{d}{L^2}
    \ge
    \frac{2q+d}{4(d+2)}
    \asymp
    \frac{2q+d}{d} =: \alpha
    $
    we obtain, after adjusting the constant $c_0$,
    $$
    \Pr\{F>1+s\}
    \le
    2e^{-c_0\alpha s^2},
    \qquad s\ge0.
    $$
    Choose $c_1>0$ sufficiently small, and suppose that $0\le\lambda\le c_1\sqrt{\alpha}.$ Since $\alpha\ge1$, after decreasing $c_1$ if necessary, we have
    $\lambda\le c_0\alpha/4$. Moreover, by Young's inequality,
    $$
    2\lambda s
    \le
    \frac{c_0\alpha}{4}s^2
    +
    \frac{4\lambda^2}{c_0\alpha}.
    $$
    Hence, for $s\ge0$, we have 
    $$
    \begin{aligned}
        \lambda(1+s)^2-c_0\alpha s^2
        =
        \lambda+2\lambda s+(\lambda-c_0\alpha)s^2
        \le
        \lambda
        +
        \frac{4\lambda^2}{c_0\alpha}
        -
        \frac{c_0\alpha}{2}s^2.
    \end{aligned}
    $$
    For $\lambda>0$, integration by parts gives
    $$
    \mathbb E e^{\lambda F^2}
    \le
    e^\lambda
    +
    2\lambda
    \int_1^\infty
    t e^{\lambda t^2}\Pr\{F>t\}\,dt.
    $$
    Writing $t=1+s$ and using the preceding tail estimate, we obtain
    $$
    \begin{aligned}
        \mathbb E e^{\lambda F^2}
    &\le
    e^\lambda
    +
    4\lambda
    \int_0^\infty
    (1+s)
    e^{\lambda(1+s)^2-c_0\alpha s^2}\,ds
    \\
    &\le
    e^\lambda
    \left[
        1+
        4e^{4\lambda^2/(c_0\alpha)}
        \lambda
        \int_0^\infty
        (1+s)e^{-c_0\alpha s^2/2}\,ds
    \right].
    \end{aligned}
    $$
    Since
    $$
    \int_0^\infty
    (1+s)e^{-c_0\alpha s^2/2}\,ds
    =
    O(\alpha^{-1/2}+\alpha^{-1})
    =
    O(\alpha^{-1/2}),
    $$
    and $\frac{\lambda^2}{\alpha}\le c_1^2$, the quantity in brackets is bounded by a constant. Thus
    $
    \mathbb E e^{\lambda F^2}
    \le
    K e^\lambda
    $
    for some absolute $K>0$. This concludes the proof.

label: prop:stochastic

name: Klartag--AGZ estimate with weights given by orbit size

title: Proof
body_md:
The dimension bound is an analogue of
    \cite[Lemma~3.3]{AbuyaGargavaZhao} that allows different orbit sizes. Since every $B\in\mathcal Q$ is $\tau$-invariant, we have $\langle B\tau x,\tau x\rangle=\langle Bx,x\rangle.$ In particular, if $x\in\partial E_{A_t}\cap\Lambda$, then
    $\tau x\in\Lambda$ and
    $$
    \langle A_t\tau x,\tau x\rangle
    =
    \langle A_tx,x\rangle
    =
    1.
    $$
    Therefore the contact set $\partial E_{A_t}\cap\Lambda$  is a union of complete $\tau$-orbits and hence 
    $$
    \left|\{\text{contact orbits}\}\right|
    =
    \sum_{x\in\partial E_{A_t}\cap\Lambda}\frac1{M_{\operatorname{supp}(x)}}.
    $$
    Each contact orbit imposes at most one independent linear condition on
    $F_{A_t}$. Hence
    $$
    \dim F_{A_t}
    \ge
    q-
    \sum_{x\in\partial E_{A_t}\cap\Lambda}\frac1{M_{\operatorname{supp}(x)}}.
    $$

    The contact estimate is proved as in
    \cite[Lemma~3.7]{AbuyaGargavaZhao}, with the constant orbit weight
    $1/m$ there replaced by $1/M_{\operatorname{supp}(x)}$.  \cref{lem:stochastic-prelim} gives
    $$
    \begin{aligned}
        \mathbb E_{\mathrm{Br}}\left[
            \mathbf1_{\mathcal G_t}
            \sum_{x\in\partial E_{A_t}\cap\Lambda}\frac1{M_{\operatorname{supp}(x)}}
        \right]
        \le
        2
        \sum_{0\ne x\in\Lambda}
        \frac1{M_{\operatorname{supp}(x)}}
        \mathbf1_{\{1-1/d\le\|x\|\le\rho_t\}}
        \Psi\left(
            \frac{a_0-\|x\|^{-2}}
            {\beta(x)\sqrt t}
        \right)
        =
        2K_t(\Lambda).
    \end{aligned}
    $$
    On $\mathcal G_t^c$, the boundary bound
    \cite[Lemma~3.1]{AbuyaGargavaZhao},
    $
    \left|\partial E_{A_t}\cap\Lambda\right|
    \le 2(2^d-1),
    $
    together with
    $\Pr_{\mathrm{Br}}(\mathcal G_t^c)\le e^{-2d}$,
    gives a contribution $e^{-cd}$.   Hence
    $$
    \mathbb E_{\mathrm{Br}}
    \sum_{x\in\partial E_{A_t}\cap\Lambda}\frac1{M_{\operatorname{supp}(x)}}
    \le
    2K_t(\Lambda)+e^{-cd}.
    $$

    Finally, we follow the proof of
    \cite[Proposition~3.5]{AbuyaGargavaZhao}.  In our notation, their
    It\^o calculation gives
    $$
    \mathbb E_{\mathrm{Br}}\log\det A_T
    \le
    -\frac12
    \int_0^T
    \mathbb E_{\mathrm{Br}}\dim F_{A_t}\,dt
    +
    O\left(
        1+\frac{qT}{d}
        +qT\sqrt{dT}
        +qTe^{-2d}
    \right),
    $$
    whenever $dT\le c$.  Substituting the dimension bound above yields
    $$
    \begin{aligned}
        \mathbb E_{\mathrm{Br}}\log\det A_T
        \le{}&
        -\frac{qT}{2}
        +
        \frac12
        \int_0^T
        \mathbb E_{\mathrm{Br}}
        \sum_{x\in\partial E_{A_t}\cap\Lambda}
        \frac1{M_{\operatorname{supp}(x)}}\,dt
        \\
             &+
             O\left(
                 1+\frac{qT}{d}
                 +qT\sqrt{dT}
                 +qTe^{-2d}
             \right),
    \end{aligned}
    $$
    as claimed.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:full-contact}
    There exists a constant $K>0$ such that, for every
    $0<t\le T$ we have 
    $$
    \mathbb E_g K_t^{\mathrm{full}}(\Lambda_g^*)
    \le
    \frac{K}{M}e^{\gamma t}.
    $$
head: environment
name: Contribution from vectors of full support

title: Proof
body_md:
Every vector of full support has orbit size $M$.  The Haar
    mean-value formula for vectors of prescribed support and the normalization
    $\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda_g^*)=v_d$ give  
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb E_g
        K_t^{\mathrm{full}}(\Lambda_g^*)
        =
        \frac1{Mv_d}
        \int_{\mathbb R^d}
        \mathbf1_{\{
                1-1/d\le\|x\|\le\rho_t
        \}}
        \Psi\left(
            \frac{
                a_0-\|x\|^{-2}
            }{
                \beta(x)\sqrt t
            }
        \right)\,dx 
        = \frac1M
        \int_{S^{d-1}}
        J_t(\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega),
    \end{align*}
    where $d\sigma$ denotes the probability measure on $S^{d-1}$ and 
    $$
    J_t(\omega)
    =
    d
    \int_{1-1/d}^{\rho_t}
    \Psi\left(
        \frac{
            a_0-r^{-2}
        }{
            \beta(\omega)\sqrt t
        }
    \right)
    r^{d-1}\,dr.
    $$
    The radial estimate from \cite[Lemma~4.1]{AbuyaGargavaZhao} implies that
    $$
    J_t(\omega)\le
    \exp\left((1+K_1\sqrt{dt})\frac{d^2t}{8}\beta(\omega)^2\right)
    $$
    for an absolute constant $K_1>0$. Set
    $$
    F(\omega)^2
    =
    \frac{d(d+2)}{2q+d}\,\beta(\omega)^2.
    $$
    Then
    $$
    \frac{d^2t}{8}\beta(\omega)^2
    =
    \gamma t F(\omega)^2.
    $$   
    Thus, with
    $
    \lambda_t
    =
    (1+K_1\sqrt{dt})\gamma t,
    $
    we have
    $
    J_t(\omega)\le e^{\lambda_tF(\omega)^2}.
    $
    By admissibility and the estimates preceding the lemma,
    $$
    \lambda_t=O(\log d),
    \qquad
    \sqrt{\frac{2q+d}{d}}\asymp\sqrt r,
    $$
    and $\log d=o(\sqrt r)$.  Hence $\lambda_t$ lies in the range of
    \cref{lem:angular}, uniformly for $0<t\le T$.  Therefore
    $$
    \int_{S^{d-1}}J_t(\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega)
    \le
    K_2e^{\lambda_t}.
    $$
    Moreover, by
    $
    \lambda_t-\gamma t
    \le
    K_1\gamma T\sqrt{dT}
    =
    o(1),
    $
    we obtain 
    $$
    \int_{S^{d-1}}J_t(\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega)
    \le
    Ke^{\gamma t}.
    $$
    This proves the result.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:packing}
    For every sufficiently large $d$ for which admissible gluing data exist,
    there is a lattice packing in $\mathbb R^d$ with density
    $$
    \Delta_d^L
    \gg
    d^2\frac{M}{C}\,2^{-d}.
    $$
head: environment

label: eq:det-final
title: Proof
body_md:
Apply \cref{prop:stochastic} to the lattice $\Lambda$ selected in 
    \cref{subsec:stochastic-selection}. Using \eqref{eq:selected-K} gives 
    $$
    \int_0^T
    \mathbb E_{\mathrm{Br}}
    \sum_{x\in\partial E_{A_t}\cap\Lambda}
    \frac1{M_{\operatorname{supp}(x)}}\,dt
    =
    O(1).
    $$
    Note that 
    $
    \frac{qT}{d}=o(1),
    $
    and, by \eqref{eq:R-stochastic-error},
    $$
    qT\sqrt{dT}
    =
    O\left(
        \frac{(\log d)^{3/2}}{\sqrt r}
    \right)
    =
    o(1).
    $$
    The remaining error term $  qTe^{-2d}$ in \eqref{eq:stochastic-det} 
    is also negligible.  Therefore \eqref{eq:stochastic-det} becomes 
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathbb E_{\mathrm{Br}}\log\det A_T
        \le
        -\frac{qT}{2}
        +O(1).
        \label{eq:det-final}
    \end{equation*}
    Hence there exists a realization for which the final ellipsoid
    $
    E=E_{A_T}
    $
    is lattice-free and
    $$
    \log\det A_T
    \le
    -\frac{qT}{2}+O(1).
    $$
    For this realization,
    $$
    \frac{\operatorname{vol}(E_{A_T})}{v_d}
    =
    (\det A_T)^{-1/2}
    \gg
    \exp\left(\frac{qT}{4}\right) =     \left(
        \frac{M\gamma}{K_0}
    \right)^{q/(4\gamma)}.
    $$
    Note that 
    $$
    \frac{q}{4\gamma}
    =
    \frac{
        2q(d+2)
    }{
        d(2q+d)
    }
    =
    1-O(r^{-1}),
    $$
    where we used $q\asymp dr$.  Moreover,
    $
    \log(M\gamma)
    =
    O(\log d)
    =
    o(r),
    $
    where the last estimate follows from the admissibility assumption $r \gg (\log d)^4 $. It follows that
    $
    (M\gamma/K_0)^{q/(4\gamma)}
    \gg
    M\gamma.
    $
    Since
    $
    \gamma\asymp q,
    $
    we conclude that
    \begin{equation}
        \operatorname{vol}(E)
        \gg
        Mq\,v_d.
        \label{eq:ellipsoid-volume}
    \end{equation}
    Finally, \eqref{eq:q} gives
    $
    q\gg Cr^2.
    $
    Since
    $
    d=Cr+a
    \le
    C(r+1)
    \le
    2Cr
    $
    for all sufficiently large $d$, we have 
    $
    Cr^2
    \gg
    \frac{d^2}{C}.
    $
    Consequently
    \begin{equation}
        Mq
        \gg
        d^2\frac{M}{C}.
        \label{eq:Mq-final}
    \end{equation}
    Because $E$ is lattice-free, the translates of $E/2$ by $\Lambda$
    have disjoint interiors.  Their packing density is
    $$
    \frac{
        \operatorname{vol}(E)
    }{
        2^d\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)
    }
    =
    \frac{
        \operatorname{vol}(E)
    }{
        2^dv_d
    }.
    $$
    Using \eqref{eq:ellipsoid-volume} and \eqref{eq:Mq-final}, we obtain
    $
    \Delta_d^L
    \gg
    d^2\frac{M}{C}\,2^{-d}.
    $
    A linear change of variables sends the ellipsoid to a Euclidean ball while
    preserving packing density.  This proves the proposition.

label: thm:deterministic-packing
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:deterministic-packing}
    Let $\bigl(\mathcal N,(y_n)_{n\in\mathcal N}\bigr)$
    be any admissible family of gluing data,
    with associated parameters $C$ and $M$.
    Then, as $d\to\infty$,
    \[
        \Delta_d^L
        \ge
        (1-o(1))\frac{dM}{eC}\,2^{-d}.
    \]
    In particular, for the admissible family
    constructed in
    \cref{thm:arithmetic-realization},
    we obtain
    \[
        \Delta_d^L
        \gg
        d\log\log d\,2^{-d}
    \]
    for every sufficiently large integer $d$.
head: environment

label: lem:minkowski-stretching
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:minkowski-stretching}
    Let $\Lambda\subset V$ be a full lattice preserved by $\tau$.
    Starting with $W_0=\{0\}$, choose a shortest vector
    $x_i\in\Lambda\setminus W_{i-1}$ and put
    $$
    \mu_i=\|x_i\|,
    \qquad
    W_i=W_{i-1}+\mathbb R[\tau]x_i.
    $$
    Continue until $W_k=V$, and set
    $$
    b_i=\dim W_i-\dim W_{i-1},
    \qquad
    \bar\mu=\prod_{i=1}^k\mu_i^{b_i/d}.
    $$
    There is a positive definite linear map $T_0$ commuting with $\tau$ such that
    $$
    \det T_0=1,
    \qquad
    \lambda_1(T_0\Lambda)=\bar\mu.
    $$
head: environment
name: Minkowski's lemma

label: lem:deterministic-stretching
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:deterministic-stretching}
    For every full $\tau$-invariant lattice $\Lambda\subset V$ and every
    $\rho>0$, there is a positive definite linear map $T$ commuting with
    $\tau$ such that
    $$
    \lambda_1(T\Lambda)\ge\rho,
    \qquad
    \log\det T\le H_\rho(\Lambda).
    $$
head: environment
name: Stretching bound for lattices preserved by the cyclic action

title: Proof
body_md:
Take $x_i,\mu_i,W_i,b_i,\bar\mu$ and $T_0$ from
    \cref{lem:minkowski-stretching}, and set
    $
    T=\frac{\rho}{\bar\mu}T_0.
    $
    Then $T$ is positive definite, commutes with $\tau$, and satisfies
    $\lambda_1(T\Lambda)=\rho$. Since $\sum_i b_i=d$, we have
    $$
    \log\det T
    =\sum_{i=1}^k b_i\log\frac{\rho}{\mu_i}
    \le\sum_{i=1}^k b_i h_\rho(x_i).
    $$
    Put $S_i=\operatorname{supp}(x_i)$. The dimension bound for
    $\mathbb R[\tau]x_i$ gives $b_i\le c_{S_i}$. The selected cyclic orbits
    are pairwise disjoint, since $x_i\notin W_{i-1}$ and $W_{i-1}$ is
    preserved by $\tau$. Each orbit contains $M_{S_i}$ vectors, all of
    support $S_i$ and length $\mu_i$. Its contribution to
    \eqref{eq:deterministic-log-sum} is therefore $c_{S_i}h_\rho(x_i)$.
    Consequently,
    $$
    \log\det T
    \le\sum_{i=1}^k c_{S_i}h_\rho(x_i)
    \le H_\rho(\Lambda).
    $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $\rho>0$ by
    $
    \rho^d=\frac{dM}{C}.
    $
    Admissibility gives $C\le d$, $r\le d$, and $\log M=O(\log d)$,
    so
    $$
    |\log\rho|=O\left(\frac{\log d}{d}\right)
    =O\left(d^{-1}+\sqrt{\frac{\log d}{r}}\right).
    $$
    Hence \eqref{eq:deterministic-mean-bound} applies.  Set
    $\epsilon_d=e^{-cr}/r$, which tends to zero.  There is a choice of
    $g$ for which
    $$
    H_\rho(\Lambda_g^*)\le1+\epsilon_d.
    $$
    Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:deterministic-stretching} to this lattice.
    By \eqref{eq:deterministic-density} and
    $\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda_g^*)=v_d$, the resulting lattice has packing density
    at least
    $$
    \frac{\rho^d}{2^d}\exp(-1-\epsilon_d)
    =e^{-\epsilon_d}\frac{dM}{eC}\,2^{-d}.
    $$
    This proves the first assertion.  Applying
    \cref{thm:arithmetic-realization}, which supplies admissible data
    with $M/C\gg\log\log d$ for every sufficiently large integer $d$,
    proves the second assertion.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
For a $\tau$-invariant ball of normalized volume $V$ (Euclidean volume
$Vv_d$), Siegel's formula gives an expected count $V$ of vectors with full support, and
this count is a multiple of $M$. The estimate for vectors of proper support then
shows that a lattice-free ball exists at $V=M-o(1)$, provided
$Me^{-cr}=o(1)$. This yields density $(M-o(1))2^{-d}$.  In the present
construction $M=d^{o(1)}$, so direct orbit counting alone does not give
$d\log\log d\,2^{-d}$.

name: Direct orbit counting

label: eq:single-field-mean
title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $K$ be a number field, let $K_\infty=K\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$,
and let $r\ge2$. Let $\mathcal O_K$ denote the ring of integers of $K$.
Put $G_K=\operatorname{SL}_r(K_\infty)$. Let
$\Lambda\subseteq K^r$ be a full $\mathbb Z$-lattice, and set
$$
\Gamma_\Lambda
=\{\gamma\in\operatorname{SL}_r(K)\mid\gamma\Lambda=\Lambda\}.
$$
The group $\Gamma_\Lambda$ is arithmetic, so $G_K/\Gamma_\Lambda$ has
finite invariant volume. Normalize this measure to have total mass
one. For every nonnegative bounded compactly supported Borel function
$f$ on $K_\infty^r$,
\begin{equation}
\int_{G_K/\Gamma_\Lambda}
\sum_{v\in g\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}f(v)\,d\mu(g)
=
\frac{1}{\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)}
\int_{K_\infty^r}f(x)\,dx.
\label{eq:single-field-mean}
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Siegel mean value theorem over a number field
